b-agora.angle_note: pointer: the meyhane night at Agora — the drink, the hour

ref_venue.name: Agora Meyhanesi
ref_venue.verdict: The meyhane as it was before the neighbourhood changed hands
ref_venue.caveat: trading seven days a week; own site agora1890.com
ref_venue.hook: Founded 1890 by a Greek captain, burned in 1955, rebuilt on the same walls.
ref_venue.person: Asteri Dulidis, a Rum (Greek) sea captain, opened it in 1890 in Balat's Çıfıtçı Çarşısı. Three generations of Dulidis kept it: Asteri, then his son Stelyo, then Stelyo's son Hristo, who left for Thessaloniki with his wife in 2001. Chef Ahmet Arı runs the meze counter today.
ref_venue.signature: The meze counter — about sixty of them, under chef Ahmet Arı. Time Out Istanbul names the favourites: yaprak ciğer, bademli kabak (courgette with almonds in garlicky yoghurt), Girit ezmesi, balık pastırması and tarama. Take the trolley slowly and let the rakı set the pace.
ref_venue.address: Balat, Mürselpaşa Cad. No:185, Fatih, 34087 İstanbul
ref_venue.price_range: ₺₺₺ — mezes are individually cheap; the rakı is what makes the bill
ref_venue.reservation: Book through the house site (agora1890.com) or by phone. It runs at 150 to 200 covers and still fills at weekends.
ref_venue.best_time: A long dinner — a meyhane evening is not a two-hour thing

signal_chip.label: TIME OUT ISTANBUL
signal_chip.full: Time Out Istanbul's entry calls it pre-Republic meyhane culture with 130 years behind it and credits chef Ahmet Arı with sixty mezes — but the page is dated 13 November 2020, so read it as a soft, ageing signal. No ranking body (MICHELIN, 50 Best, Gault&Millau) lists it.

dishes.name: Bademli kabak
dishes.note: courgette with almonds and garlicky yoghurt

charter.book: Site (agora1890.com) or phone · 150–200 covers · fills at weekends
charter.fit: The safe big-table call: a 135-year meyhane that can seat a party tonight and still feel like Istanbul.

old_cards.name: Agora Meyhanesi 1890
old_cards.teaser: A Greek captain's tavern in Balat — still open, its community long gone.
old_cards.body: Asteri Dulidis, a Greek sea captain, opened it in 1890; his son Stelyo and then his grandson Hristo Dulidis ran it after him, three generations of one family on one street. The barrel tables are the original format — wine drawn straight off a cask — which is what a meyhane was before anyone made it picturesque. Restored in 2013 by the architect Hakan Kıran, trading seven days. The sign, the family name and the neighbourhood still agree with each other. Balat, Fatih · open daily, built for long dinners

b-sofra.angle_note: the pacing of the meyhane table, told once

old_cards.name: The rakı sofrası
old_cards.teaser: Not a drink with dinner — a table that paces food across an evening.
old_cards.body: Under the Turkish Food Codex, rakı is suma — grape or raisin distillate — redistilled with Pimpinella anisum in traditional copper pot stills of no more than 5,000 litres, bottled at 40 per cent minimum. Water turns it white: aslan sütü , lion's milk. The order is fixed. Cold mezes first and held a long time, then hot, then the fish. You drink at the speed of the table and never without food. Ordering rakı and eating fast is the visitor's giveaway. Any meyhane · Thursday is the night

old_cards.name: The meyhane table
old_cards.teaser: Cold mezes, then hot, then fish — a drinking licence that was never Muslim.
old_cards.body: Alcohol was forbidden to Muslims, so the keeping of a drinking house fell in practice almost entirely to Greeks, Armenians and Jews. That is why the meyhane looks as it does: the long table of cold mezes before the hot, rakı cut with water until it turns white, fasıl players moving between tables. The wealth tax of 1942, the pogrom of September 1955 and the measures of 1964 removed the authors. The form stayed. Asmalımescit and Nevizade in Beyoğlu; Balat and Kadıköy for the quieter version

b-stambouli.angle_note: opened Aug 2026 per old card; status per venue re-check

old_cards.name: Lokanta Stambouli
old_cards.teaser: A Rum meyhane reopening in Pera in 2026 is not a neutral act.
old_cards.body: Perviz Resuli has opened it on the first floor of the old Union Française building inside Minoa Pera — a deliberately plain meyhane card of cold mezes, hot mezes and the day's fish, and a room built for talking rather than for music. It works the Turkish and the Rum (Ottoman Greek) traditions together instead of choosing. Read against the 1942 wealth tax, the 1955 pogrom and the 1964 expulsions, it is the most loaded opening in the city. It opened in the first week of August 2026, so go knowing there is no track record behind it yet. Meşrutiyet Cad. 99, Asmalımescit, Beyoğlu

old_cards.group: Natural wine and the caves à manger
old_cards.name: WAYANA Wine Bar & Tapas
old_cards.teaser: Every one of 500-plus labels open by the glass. Nowhere else does this.
old_cards.body: Moda, and the single most useful room in Istanbul for anyone who thinks Turkish wine means a hotel Cabernet. The house carries labels from 143 Turkish wineries and, as of July 2026, ninety endemic grape varieties — and serves the entire list by the glass, which is the whole point: you can taste eight native grapes in one evening instead of gambling a bottle on one. Tapas alongside, built to pair rather than to fill. Start here and the rest of the guide reads differently. Ferit Tek Sok. 60/B, Moda, Kadıköy · 16:00–00:00, weekends from 14:00

old_cards.name: Solera Winery
old_cards.teaser: An all-Turkish list in a narrow Beyoğlu room, 300 metres off İstiklal.
old_cards.body: Opened 1 October 2011 on Yeni Çarşı Caddesi and pours only domestic producers — red, white, rosé, sparkling and fruit wine, no imports on the card. Since 2013 the house has farmed its own vineyard at Gaziköy in Tekirdağ, on the Marmara shore of Thrace, and runs its own Şarap Tadımı tasting evenings walking guests through Turkish varieties region by region. This is the room where the argument that Turkey has a wine culture rather than a wine industry gets made in glasses rather than in print. The Thracian producers you will meet here — Chamlija, founded 2007 by Mustafa Çamlıca on the decomposed granite of the Strandja massif in Kırklareli, labels drawn by his daughter İrem — are farming indigenous Papazkarası alongside the international grapes the domestic market once demanded. The tell — Ask for the by-the-glass flight of native grapes rather than a bottle: Öküzgözü and Boğazkere from the east, Narince from Tokat, Papazkarası from Thrace. Kitchen runs to cheese and charcuterie boards, salads, pasta and köfte if you want to stay. Tomtom Mah., Yeni Çarşı Cad. No:44, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Daily 13:00–01:00

old_cards.name: Sensus Wine Boutique
old_cards.teaser: A stone cellar at the foot of the Galata Tower that sells the cheese as seriously as the wine.
old_cards.body: The Galata room on Büyük Hendek Caddesi was the first; the business now runs thirteen shops across Türkiye, from Kavaklıdere in Ankara to Çeşme, Bursa and İzmir, and says so on its own site. The buying is done on quarterly tasting tours through seven Turkish wine regions, direct from boutique producers, and the same trips bring back the cheese, charcuterie, honey, olives and oil that fill the counter. It is a shop that lets you sit down, not a bar with a shelf — which is why the pairing plate is the point rather than an afterthought. Time Out Istanbul has carried it for years as the Turkish wine-and-cheese address by the tower. The tell — Order a tasting flight against a regional cheese plate — the counter cuts from producers the buyers have actually visited. Take a bottle away afterwards; the retail price is the reason to buy here rather than drink here. Bereketzade Mah., Kuledibi, Büyük Hendek Cad. No:5, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Not published on the house site — call ahead

old_cards.name: Öküzgözü & Boğazkere
old_cards.teaser: The bull's eye and the throat-scraper — Turkey's great red pairing, rarely poured apart.
old_cards.body: Öküzgözü, 'bull's eye', comes from the villages around Elazığ and Malatya: violets, red and black plum, soft ripe tannin, medium-bodied and generous, and capable of oak without collapsing. Boğazkere grows down the Tigris from Diyarbakır and is its opposite — dense, structural, aggressively tannic, the name meaning roughly 'throat-scraper'. Blended, the first sands down the second, and that blend is what Turkey exports as its own idea. Order each on its own once, to hear what it was actually contributing. Elazığ, Malatya and Diyarbakır

b-light-reds.angle_note: the light reds and rosés in one card

old_cards.name: Kalecik Karası
old_cards.teaser: The Anatolian red that drinks like Gamay, and was nearly lost.
old_cards.body: From Kalecik, north-east of Ankara on the Kızılırmak. Pale to medium in colour, red cherry and strawberry, low to moderate tannin — and Turkish drinkers reach almost automatically for Gamay or Pinot Noir to describe it, which tells you exactly what it is for. This is the bottle when the table is eating mezes rather than grilled meat. Serve it cool. In a country whose reputation abroad rests on tannin, it is the standing argument for the other direction. Kalecik, Ankara province

old_cards.name: Papazkarası & Çalkarası
old_cards.teaser: The two that make the country's best rosés, from opposite ends of it.
old_cards.body: Papazkarası — 'priest's black' — is Thracian, thick-skinned, high in acid and modest in tannin, now vinified as a varietal red, as blanc de noirs and as traditional-method sparkling. Çalkarası comes from the Çal district of Denizli in the inland Aegean and reaches its best as rosé: pale, dry, sharply acidic, tart cherry and pomegranate where a Provençal wine would give melon. Both are summer bottles, both are improving fast, and both are still priced as curiosities rather than as serious wine. Thrace and Denizli

old_cards.name: Narince & Emir
old_cards.teaser: One means 'delicately'; the other grows on Cappadocian volcanic rock.
old_cards.body: Narince is Tokat's grape and its name means 'delicately' — aromatic, medium to full-bodied, with a texture that carries oak without losing the fruit. Emir comes off the volcanic soils of Cappadocia: high acid, mineral and savoury, sharper and more austere than Narince, and the one with real ageing capacity. Between them they cover the entire Turkish white argument, and both are absurdly cheap set against any European equivalent. Emir with fish and raw things, Narince with anything out of a wood oven. Tokat and Cappadocia

b-mikla-bar.angle_note: pointer: the bar terrace without the tasting menu

ref_venue.name: Mikla
ref_venue.neighborhood: Beyoğlu — roof of the Marmara Pera
ref_venue.verdict: The view is famous; the ingredient philosophy is why it lasted
ref_venue.caveat: ★ in the MICHELIN Guide Türkiye 2026; top two floors of The Marmara Pera
ref_venue.why: Chef Mehmet Gürs. The house that invented the phrase New Anatolian Kitchen and spent fifteen years proving it meant something.
ref_venue.hook: Rooftop on the 18th floor of The Marmara Pera, open since October 2005.
ref_venue.cosign: MICHELIN Guide Türkiye 2026 (one Star); The World's 50 Best Discovery; Gault&Millau Türkiye 15.5/20
ref_venue.signature: Smoked lamb loin with charred endive and apple molasses is the plate the house is judged on; fried hamsi — anchovy — with a Cappadocian white is the other. Both are the dishes The World's 50 Best Discovery names.
ref_venue.address: The Marmara Pera, Meşrutiyet Caddesi No:15, 18th floor, Tepebaşı, 34430 Beyoğlu, İstanbul
ref_venue.price_range: ₺₺₺₺ — Mikla Tasting (six courses) ₺10,500; vegan tasting (seven courses) ₺9,600; three-course prix fixe ₺8,500. Wine pairings with the tasting ₺5,500 or ₺8,000; a three-glass à la carte pairing ₺3,200. VAT included, service extra (house menu read August 2026).
ref_venue.reservation: Online; confirmation comes by email. Cancel at least eight hours ahead, and arrive on time — the house cancels the table thirty minutes after your slot.
ref_venue.best_time: Sit down by 19:30 for the light; the kitchen stops taking food orders at 21:30

dishes.name: Fried hamsi
dishes.note: anchovy, paired with a crisp Cappadocian white

guest.dress: Stated in the house booking flow: 'In accordance with our Smart Chic clothing policy, sportswear such as tracksuits and slippers are not accepted.'
guest.view_terrace: At the top of The Marmara Pera: the restaurant plus a roof-terrace bar (open 18:00–02:00) 'in the midst of jasmine scents accompanied by the chilling breeze of Galata'; The World's 50 Best says 'come to Mikla for the best-in-Istanbul views'. No specific floor number is published by the house.
guest.max_party: 8 online; 'more than 8 people, please call +90 (212) 293 5656 or send an e-mail to reservations@miklarestaurant.com' per the booking flow.
guest.booking_lead: No published booking window; the online diary takes a credit-card guarantee of 35 EUR per person ('no charges will be made unless there is a no-show'), cancellation at least 8 h ahead, and the table is cancelled 30 minutes after the slot if you have not arrived (booking flow and rules pages read 2026-08-16).
guest.guest_line: Mikla (1-star, rooftop of The Marmara Pera, Mon–Sat dinner only from 18:00): New Anatolian cooking with the city's most famous rooftop view and a terrace bar until 02:00 — smart-chic dress, last food order 21:30, parties over 8 by phone or email.

charter.book: Online · card guarantee €35/head · parties over 8 by phone
charter.view: Rooftop of The Marmara Pera — the famous view · terrace bar to 02:00
charter.fit: The view table: twenty years of New Anatolian cooking above Pera.

old_cards.group: Looking back at the old city
old_cards.name: Mikla Bar
old_cards.teaser: The starred kitchen is downstairs; the terrace will pour you a drink without it.
old_cards.body: Mehmet Gürs's restaurant holds a MICHELIN star and occupies the top two floors of The Marmara Pera, but the bar is a separate proposition. It opens at 18:00 and runs to 02:00, has an outdoor terrace and a pool, and does not require the tasting menu — you can sit at it for the price of a cocktail. It is the highest roof on Meşrutiyet Caddesi, which is most of what you are paying for. The Marmara Pera, Meşrutiyet Cad., Beyoğlu · bar 18:00–02:00 · around TL 700–850 a cocktail

old_cards.group: The other shore, and the strait
old_cards.name: Roof Mezzepotamia
old_cards.teaser: The one every English guide puts on the wrong shore.
old_cards.body: It is in Sirkeci, on the historic peninsula, on the terrace of the Orient Occident Hotel — not Karaköy, where a run of English-language listings puts it. The difference is the whole point: from here you look back at Galata instead of out from it, across 270 degrees of the Bosphorus, the Golden Horn and the tower. The name folds mezze into Mesopotamia, and the kitchen runs the seven regions of Turkey. Sirkeci Station, terminus of the Orient Express from 1890, is a few doors away. Orient Occident Hotel, Hobyar Mah., Aşirefendi Cad. No:11, Sirkeci, Fatih · book for sunset · around TL 750–900 a cocktail

b-before-roof.angle_note: no place: the price, the hour (never a perishable sunset time), the season

old_cards.name: What a drink costs up there
old_cards.teaser: You are buying the sightline. The drink is incidental.
old_cards.body: Budget roughly 600 to 900 TL for a cocktail at a mainstream hotel rooftop in 2026. The marquee addresses sit above that band — current listings for the best-known Karaköy and Pera terraces run 1,000 to 1,200 TL a cocktail, The Bank Roof Bar among them. The gap between the two bands is the view, not the liquor. 2026 prices, and they move with the lira — treat them as an order of magnitude, not a quote

old_cards.name: The hour
old_cards.teaser: Turkey never puts its clocks back, so the light lasts absurdly late.
old_cards.body: Turkey abolished daylight saving on 7 September 2016 and has stayed on UTC+3 ever since, an hour ahead of its own longitude. The effect on a roof is direct: mid-August sunset falls around 20:05, with the golden hour from about 19:25 and blue light holding to about 20:35. By midwinter the same moment arrives just before 17:40. Arrive at least forty-five minutes early if you want a table on the rail. Mid-August sunset around 20:05 · winter solstice sunset 17:40

old_cards.name: The season
old_cards.teaser: Half these roofs simply are not there in winter.
old_cards.body: An Istanbul rooftop is a summer business. Terraces glass themselves in, cut their hours or close outright from about November, and the listings do not always keep up — Sky Karaköy carries a Seasonally Closed label on its own group's site, and Manifest advertises its glass ceiling precisely because staying open through the cold is unusual here. Between November and March, telephone the venue on the day. A confirmed booking is not proof the roof is trading. Roughly November to March · phone on the day, not the week before

b-pera-palace.angle_note: one home for the Pera Palace: the bar and the domed saloon's tea

old_cards.name: Orient Bar, Pera Palace
old_cards.teaser: The lobby-floor bar of the hotel built in 1892 for passengers off the Orient Express — currently dark for the season.
old_cards.body: As of this check the hotel's own page states the Orient Bar is out of service until the end of the summer season, so do not walk up expecting it. What is open in its place is the Orient Terrace on the ground floor, lobby side, over the Golden Horn: 09:00 to 23:00 for the full menu and 23:00 to 02:00 for drinks only. Upstairs, Room 411 is kept as the Agatha Christie room — 46 square metres of period furniture, a library of her books in several languages and a replica of her typewriter, and it is bookable as a guest room rather than roped off as a museum. Smart casual on the terrace; the hotel enforces it. The tell — Since the bar itself is shut, take the terrace at dusk for the Golden Horn light and the fresh-fruit cocktails, and ask at reception whether 411 is free to look at. Meşrutiyet Cad. No:52, Tepebaşı, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Orient Bar: closed until end of summer season. Orient Terrace: daily 09:00–23:00, drinks to 02:00 Heads up — A limited run — check the end date before you plan around it.

old_cards.name: Kubbeli Lounge, Pera Palace
old_cards.teaser: Afternoon tea under the domes, with a pianist named on the hotel's own page.
old_cards.body: The Kubbeli — kubbe is Turkish for dome — is the high-ceilinged salon the hotel built its social life around, and it is the room to use while the Orient Bar is shut. The house lists traditional afternoon tea accompanied by the piano of Aslı Güral, which is unusual: hotels rarely name the musician. Daylight through the high windows is the whole design brief of the room, so it reads completely differently at four in the afternoon than the bar does at eleven at night. It is a hotel salon, priced as one. The tell — Traditional afternoon tea, taken in daylight, in the salon rather than on the terrace. Book it; walk-ins compete with hotel guests. Pera Palace Hotel, Meşrutiyet Cad. No:52, Tepebaşı, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Afternoon tea service — hours not published, book ahead

old_cards.name: Kubbeli Saloon, Pera Palace
old_cards.teaser: Built for people who had just spent three days on a train.
old_cards.body: Vallaury again: he began the hotel in 1892 and it opened in 1895, built to lodge Orient Express passengers arriving off the Paris run. It carried the first electric lift in Constantinople — reportedly the second in Europe — and Atatürk's Room 101 is kept as a museum room. The domed saloon pours a traditional afternoon tea every day from three until six, with live piano. It is priced the way a grand hotel prices things: an hour of reading and correspondence, not a working day. Meşrutiyet Caddesi, Tepebaşı, Beyoğlu · afternoon tea daily 15:00–18:00

old_cards.name: Le Fumoir and C Lounge, Çırağan Palace Kempinski
old_cards.teaser: Two bars inside a nineteenth-century Ottoman palace on the Bosphorus, with a dress code each.
old_cards.body: The hotel runs its drinking rooms as separate registers and publishes the code for each: Le Fumoir takes bar snacks at smart casual, C Lounge is the casual bar, Çırağan Bar handles refined spirits and cocktails at chic casual, and Gazebo is the lobby lounge, an Ottoman-garden conceit with the water in front of it. Tuğra, the palace's Turkish fine-dining room, is the formal end of the same building. Worth knowing before you plan an evening on the European shore: Rüya İstanbul, which appears elsewhere in this guide as a new-wave Anatolian kitchen, is also inside this hotel. The palace was the imperial residence before it was a hotel, and the terrace sits directly on the strait rather than above it. The tell — Le Fumoir for the cigar-and-snack register, C Lounge if you want to stay casual, Gazebo if you want the lobby and the garden view. Check the dress code for the specific room before you leave, not on arrival. Çırağan Cad., Yıldız Mah., Beşiktaş, İstanbul · Not published per venue — call the hotel

old_cards.name: FLUX
old_cards.teaser: Funktion-One in Maslak, and the two nights are deliberately not the same night.
old_cards.body: An RX Istanbul project in a modular room that scales from fifty to five hundred indoors plus a two-hundred-capacity terrace, on Funktion-One. The programming split is explicit and worth planning around: Fridays run house , groove-led and rhythmic; Saturdays go techno , deeper and harder. The opening season, autumn 2025, carried Ben Klock, Anja Schneider, Cormac, Setaoc Mass and Stef Mendesidis; 2026 has run to Rødhåd, Regal, Tommy Four Seven, Adriana Lopez and FJAAK. This is the serious room, and it is a long way north — budget for the taxi. Maslak, Sarıyer · late

old_cards.name: Şahika
old_cards.teaser: Multi-level in Beyoğlu, roof terrace on top, the odd end of the programming.
old_cards.body: Several floors climbing to a rooftop terrace, and the place to go when four-to-the-floor is not what you want: jungle and footwork alongside techno and house, local selectors with European guests, and exhibitions, talks and performances sharing the same building. Queer-friendly by reputation and in practice, which in this city is a specific and not automatic thing to be. Start on the roof at the end of the light and work downwards as it gets louder. Beyoğlu

old_cards.name: Suma Han
old_cards.teaser: A Greek-built rakı distillery, now an artists' building with a club inside.
old_cards.body: Built in 1923 by the Greek architect Simotas and worked as a rakı distillation plant. Bought in 2003, restored, and reopened in 2009 as offices, artist studios, residences and common rooms with a club floor and genuine acoustics folded in — two stages, techno and psy-trance, plus exhibitions and talks. That the city's clearest case of artists building their own infrastructure sits inside a Greek-built rakı works is not a coincidence this guide is going to let pass. Beyoğlu

old_cards.group: Listening bars and the hi-fi turn
old_cards.name: Arkaoda
old_cards.teaser: Kadıköy's anchor since 1999, and the only one with a Berlin offshoot.
old_cards.body: Opened on Kadife Sokak in 1999 and functionally a collective rather than a bar: selectors move between Turkish psych, jazz and electronic across a night, there is a garden, and the booking leans towards independent artists nobody is paying to put on. Its Neukölln offshoot runs on the same principle, which makes this the rare Istanbul room that exported rather than imported. Open from midday to two, which means you can start an evening here and never leave. Kadife Sok. 18/1, Caferağa, Kadıköy · 12:00–02:00

n-karga.angle_note: status: closing_soon in Aug — say what the re-check found

old_cards.group: Listening bars and the hi-fi turn
old_cards.name: Karga
old_cards.teaser: Five floors of an old wooden house, and thirty years of the Kadıköy alternative scene inside it.
old_cards.body: Trading since 1996 in a five-storey wooden house on Kadife Sokak, with KargART — concerts, screenings, exhibitions — on the top two floors and vinyl sessions in the small rooms below. It is the building the Kadıköy alternative scene grew up inside. The programme turns over constantly and lives on the venue's Instagram rather than on its website, which is a blank splash page: check the feed for what is on the night you go. Kadife Sok. 16, Caferağa, Kadıköy · programme on Instagram

n-dama.angle_note: one home for Dama: coffee by day, hi-fi at night

old_cards.group: Listening bars and the hi-fi turn
old_cards.name: Dama
old_cards.teaser: Filter coffee by day, vinyl through serious speakers once the light goes.
old_cards.body: Şakayık Sokak in Teşvikiye, and its own line is 'café by day, hi-fi by night'. Mornings are filter coffee, breakfast and laptops on a quiet side street; the evening hands the room to vinyl through a system somebody clearly spent real money on, with an open kitchen, ceramic surfaces and shelves of records. Short seasonal cocktail list, small plates. The cleanest single example of the format Istanbul has adopted faster than anywhere else. Şakayık Sok. 19, Teşvikiye, Şişli

old_cards.name: Dama
old_cards.tag: Café by day · hi-fi by night
old_cards.teaser: Filter coffee and laptops until the record shelf takes the room back.
old_cards.body: On a Teşvikiye side street: open kitchen, ceramic surfaces, shelves of records, breakfast from nine, and enough tolerance for a laptop that the neighbourhood works here. Come evening the same room becomes a hi-fi bar — vinyl through proper equipment, DJs, cocktails built on things like macadamia and banana. Istanbul has taken to the listening-bar format faster than any other European city, and Dama is where you can watch the switch happen in one afternoon. Teşvikiye, Şakayık Sok. 19, Şişli · breakfast 09:00–13:00 weekdays, to 14:00 at weekends · no reservations

old_cards.name: Kontra Plak
old_cards.teaser: An independent record shop trading on Yeni Çarşı since 2012, with a listening-room programme attached.
old_cards.body: Two doors from Galatasaray Lisesi on the street that has quietly become Beyoğlu's record row, Kontra carries new and second-hand Turkish and foreign vinyl, CDs, cassettes and music books in both Turkish and English, plus turntables, cartridges and headshells. Its own site was showing arrivals dated August 2026 when this guide checked, which is the only proof of life that matters for a shop. It runs named strands rather than one-off events — Dinleme Odası, the listening room; Kontra'da; Örümcek; Just Kids — and takes part in Record Store Day with in-store concerts. Context for why this matters: Lale Plak, open on Galip Dede Caddesi since 1954 and the shop where local musicians met, announced its closure by tweet and shut on 31 December 2019. Its owner Hakan Atala told Hürriyet the following January, "Burası müzisyenlerin buluşma yeriydi, içim buruk." The tell — Ask for the Turkish second-hand racks, not the reissue wall — the 1970s Anadolu pressings are the reason to be in this room rather than online. Time a visit to a Dinleme Odası night if the calendar allows. Tomtom Mah., Yeni Çarşı Cad. No:60/A, Galatasaray, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Daily 11:00–20:00

old_cards.name: Analog Kültür
old_cards.teaser: A record shop and studio on a Şahkulu cul-de-sac that also cuts one-off lathe records.
old_cards.body: It opened on Record Store Day 2014, when DJ and producer Kaan Düzarat went looking for somewhere to move his studio and decided the studio should be a record shop too. His reasoning, in his own words: in late 2013 there were very few shops in the city and none where you could reliably find good electronic music, old or new, so he built a room to share whatever passed his own filter. About eighty percent of the archive is second-hand — 45s and albums from the seventies and eighties, house, techno, drum and bass, synthwave and krautrock from the nineties and 2000s, then jazz, funk, soul, bossa, Middle and Far Eastern records, rock and classical. The shop also carries a proper hi-fi department (amplifiers, turntables, cartridges, reel-to-reel, speakers) and, with Eazycut Records, cuts lathe records to order. Coffee is part of the deal. The tell — Bring a recording you want on vinyl and ask about the lathe cut — call between 12:00 and 20:00. Otherwise dig the Turkish section; Düzarat has been actively buying domestic pressings as local production revived. Şahkulu, Seraskerci Çk. No:4 D:A, 34421 Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Lathe-cut enquiries 12:00–20:00; shop hours not published

old_cards.name: Akmar Pasajı
old_cards.teaser: The Kadıköy arcade that has been the city's second-hand book and record warren since 1982.
old_cards.body: It stands on the site of the Özel Marmara Koleji, a school founded in 1957 whose building was damaged by adjacent construction in 1980, demolished, and replaced in 1982 by an office block with shops on the lower floors. The name is a splice: Akdik, the owning family's surname, and syllables lifted from the school's. It runs through between Mühürdar Caddesi and Neşet Ömer Sokak, which is why half of Kadıköy uses it as a shortcut without ever stopping, and it holds a specific place in Istanbul's fanzine, metal and rock history — enough that in 1999 it was subject to a police raid on unfounded claims, with those arrested later found to have no connection to the matter. Second-hand booksellers dominate; music shops sit among them. The tell — Go for the sahaf stalls and the two music shops rather than a specific address — individual tenants turn over, the arcade does not. Walk in from Mühürdar and out onto Neşet Ömer. Caferağa Mah., Mühürdar Cad., Akmar Pasajı, Kadıköy, İstanbul · Shop hours vary by tenant

old_cards.group: The collectives and the club nights
old_cards.name: Nardis Jazz Club
old_cards.teaser: The city's longest-running dedicated jazz club, below Galata Tower.
old_cards.body: Roughly 120 seats at the foot of the Galata Tower, live jazz from local and international acts practically every night. Programming already listed into 2026–27. THE jazz room in Istanbul, and the reason Wednesday is on the week grid Kuledibi Sok., Galata, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Weekdays 21:30–00:30 · weekends 22:30–01:30

old_cards.name: Tarihi Cumhuriyet Meyhanesi
old_cards.teaser: A Balık Pazarı meyhane with live Turkish music every night and a table that has been reserved since 1938.
old_cards.body: The house was founded before the Republic was declared and, by its own account, was named by Atatürk himself — take that as the family's claim, not a documented fact, but the table it says he sat at is still kept permanently reserved, and the house has traded under the name since 1923. It is one street off the Beyoğlu fish market on Sahne Sokak, open every day from noon to midnight, with Turkish traditional live music listed as a standing feature rather than a weekend booking. The meze card carries the old Istanbul minority repertoire that most of Beyoğlu has quietly dropped: topik with caramelised onion and cinnamon, çiroz cut with dill and vinegar, kabak çiçeği dolması from Aegean flowers. The tell — Start with topik and çiroz — the Armenian and Greek plates are the reason to be in this room rather than a newer meyhane. Go late enough that the musicians are working the tables; the rakı is poured with water, not over it. Kamer Hatun Cad., Sahne Sok. No:27, Balık Pazarı, Beyoğlu, İstanbul · Daily 12:00–00:00

old_cards.name: Babylon
old_cards.teaser: The city's long-running live room in the old Bomonti brewery quarter, booking hard through winter 2026.
old_cards.body: Time Out Istanbul calls it the city's premier live music venue, and the programme backs it rather than the reputation carrying it: at this check the calendar ran from the Babylon Soundgarden Festival at Bonus Parkorman on 22 and 23 August through Ben LaMar Gay Ensemble on 1 October, Yazmin Lacey on 7 October, Kassa Overall on 9 October, the Samora Pinderhughes Quintet with Elena Pinderhughes on 10 October, Kelly Lee Owens DJ set on 16 October, and Bilal marking twenty-five years of 1st Born Second on 11 December. That is a jazz and left-field booking policy, not a covers room. It sits on Silahşör Caddesi in Bomonti, which it did as much as anything to turn into a nightlife district when it moved out of Beyoğlu. The tell — Buy the ticket before you travel — these are single-night international bookings, not a residency. Check whether the date is at Babylon itself or out at Bonus Parkorman; the festival dates are not in the venue. Silahşör Cad., Cumhuriyet Mah., Bomonti, Şişli, İstanbul · By event
